overview.text: Catalonia is a region in northeastern Spain, between the Mediterranean Sea and the Pyrenees, with Barcelona as its capital. It is one of Spain’s autonomous communities: under its Statute of Autonomy, it has its own parliament and government, called the Generalitat, and manages some public affairs while remaining within the Spanish state. Catalan, a Romance language, is a defining feature of Catalan identity and is official alongside Spanish; Aranese is also official in the region. Catalonia’s language, culture and institutional tradition distinguish it within Spain, and its distinct identity has figured prominently in a long-running movement for independence.

key_facts.text: Catalonia borders France and Andorra to the north and the Mediterranean Sea to the east; Barcelona is its capital.
The Generalitat’s institutions include Catalonia’s parliament, president and government. The Statute of Autonomy sets out their powers and relations with the Spanish state.
Catalan developed from Latin between the 8th and 10th centuries. It is also spoken beyond Catalonia, including in Andorra and the Balearic Islands.
Catalan, Spanish and Aranese are official languages in Catalonia.
Catalonia’s National Day on September 11 commemorates the loss of Catalan liberties and institutions after the 1714 defeat in the War of the Spanish Succession.
